displayQuote: Not one shred of evidence exists that life is serious

meta.title: Who really said "Not one shred of evidence exists that life is serious"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Joseph Campbell. Brendan Gill wrote it in Here at The New Yorker (1975). Campbell’s name was attached to a streamlined version on Usenet in 1993.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Not one shred of evidence exists that life is serious'?
meta.ogDescription: Quote Investigator traces it to Brendan Gill’s 1975 memoir, page 49 — where the word is ‘argument’. The Campbell credit dates from a 1993 Usenet post.

answer.label: Not Joseph Campbell — actually Brendan Gill
answer.authorDates: 1914–1997 · New Yorker writer and critic for six decades
answer.sourceLine: Brendan Gill wrote the sentence in his 1975 memoir Here at The New Yorker (Random House), chapter 6, page 49 — but with a different noun and a qualifier attached: ‘in favor of the argument that life is serious, though it is often hard and even terrible’. The trimmed ten-word wording quoted here was pinned on Joseph Campbell in a Usenet message of 29 March 1993, after Campbell’s death in 1987 (Quote Investigator ↗).

source.excerpt: In fact, not a shred of evidence exists in favor of the argument that life is serious, though it is often hard and even terrible.
trail: 1975 — Brendan Gill publishes Here at The New Yorker with Random House. On page 49 of chapter 6 he writes the sentence, with the qualifier ‘though it is often hard and even terrible’ attached; Quote Investigator verified the page on paper (Quote Investigator ↗). The first edition is scanned at the Internet Archive ↗.

1979 — John Peers’s compilation 1,001 Logical Laws prints it on page 120 as ‘Gill’s Law’, with ‘idea’ substituted for Gill’s ‘argument’ and the qualifier dropped. This is the version most quote sites still carry (Quote Investigator ↗).

29 March 1993 — a message in the Usenet newsgroup rec.games.diplomacy carries a further-streamlined ten-word version — the wording asked about here — credited to Joseph Campbell. It is the earliest Campbell-credited instance Quote Investigator cites (Quote Investigator ↗).

By January 2010 — Wayback Machine captures cited by Quote Investigator show yet another variant circulating under Ogden Nash’s name; QI notes it was probably in circulation considerably earlier (Quote Investigator ↗).
source.excerptNote: Gill’s sentence opens the passage he is best remembered for: it runs on into a short set of ‘rules of life’ drawn from the fact that everything ends in death. The 1975 book is still under copyright, so only the sentence under examination is reproduced here; the full paragraph is transcribed at Quote Investigator ↗.

author.name: Brendan Gill
author.heading: About Brendan Gill
author.metaLine: 1914–1997 · New Yorker writer, drama and architecture critic
author.bio: Brendan Gill joined The New Yorker in 1936 and stayed for more than sixty years, writing over 1,200 pieces — Profiles, Talk of the Town, and years of Broadway and Off-Broadway reviewing — before serving as the magazine’s principal architecture critic and author of its Skyline column from 1987 to 1996. Away from the desk he was one of New York’s most effective preservationists, joining Jacqueline Kennedy’s coalition to save Grand Central Terminal and chairing both the Municipal Art Society and the New York Landmarks Conservancy. Here at The New Yorker (1975), the memoir that carries this sentence, is the book he is still most quoted from — usually with someone else’s name attached.

misattribution.heading: Four names, none of them the author
misattribution.intro: This sentence has been credited to a mythographer, a light-verse poet and a German philosopher — and even the version credited to the right man has the wrong word in it. Each variant is a further edit of one paragraph written in 1975.

items.why: The streamlined form — ‘Not one shred of evidence exists that life is serious’ — is first documented in a message to the newsgroup rec.games.diplomacy dated 29 March 1993, where it carries Campbell’s name and no source (Quote Investigator ↗). Campbell died in 1987, and the line is absent from Wikiquote’s Joseph Campbell page ↗ altogether — it is not even listed among his disputed quotations.

A third variant — ‘There is not a shred of evidence that life is serious’ — was circulating under Nash’s name by January 2010 according to Wayback Machine captures, and Quote Investigator notes it was probably in circulation considerably earlier (Quote Investigator ↗). Nash died in 1971, and Wikiquote ↗ does not record the line for him.

The anonymous variant ‘Not one shred of evidence supports the notion that life is serious’ sits on Goodreads ↗ under Nietzsche’s name with no book, essay or year cited. Goodreads notes on that same page that its quotations are added by users and are not verified.

The form usually reproduced — ‘in favor of the idea that life is serious’ — is still not what Gill wrote. He wrote argument, and he did not stop there. The substitution is documented as far back as John Peers’s 1979 compilation 1,001 Logical Laws, which prints it on page 120 under the heading ‘Gill’s Law’ with the qualifier removed (Quote Investigator ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: The sentence is Brendan Gill’s, from Here at The New Yorker (Random House, 1975), chapter 6, page 49 — and in Gill’s own words the phrase runs ‘in favor of the argument that life is serious, though it is often hard and even terrible’, a page Quote Investigator verified on paper (Quote Investigator ↗).

context.heading: A joke that outgrew its author
lead: The line survives because it is a good joke with a sting in it, and because it is short enough to fit on a fridge magnet. Both qualities also make it easy to detach from whoever wrote it. Brendan Gill was a New Yorker writer with six decades at the magazine, and he set the sentence down in 1975 as the opening move of a small, cheerfully bleak argument — that since everything ends in death, the first rule of life is to enjoy it and the second is to hurt as few people as possible while you do.

What travelled was not Gill’s sentence but a series of improvements on it. A 1979 aphorism collection swapped ‘argument’ for ‘idea’ and rebranded it ‘Gill’s Law’. By 1993 a Usenet poster had cut the qualifier and the attribution both, and hung the remainder on Joseph Campbell — a mythographer in whose published work nobody has since located it (Quote Investigator ↗).
context.detailsSummary: Why the Campbell version is the one that stuck
detailsBody: Each hop made the line punchier and less traceable. Gill’s original is a clause inside a longer thought, hedged by an admission that life is often hard and even terrible. John Peers’s 1979 compilation cut the hedge and made it a ‘law’. The 1993 Usenet version cut it again, down to ten words. A shorter sentence carries further and holds an author’s name more loosely.

Joseph Campbell was a plausible host for it. He was an American professor and writer known above all for comparative mythology and comparative religion — a man associated with story, symbol and the limits of literal fact — so a one-line dismissal of seriousness sounds like something he might have said. That is the usual mechanism: a quotation drifts towards the best-known name it could credibly belong to, and Gill, a working magazine writer, was never going to win that contest.
context.pull: Gill wrote ‘argument’, and added that life is often hard and even terrible. Everything after that is other people’s editing.

sourcesVerified.claim: Brendan Gill wrote "In fact, not a shred of evidence exists in favor of the argument that life is serious, though it is often hard and even terrible" in Here at The New Yorker (Random House, New York, 1975), chapter 6, page 49, verified on paper; John Peers's 1979 compilation 1,001 Logical Laws printed it on page 120 as "Gill's Law" with "idea" replacing "argument"; a Usenet message to rec.games.diplomacy dated 29 March 1993 credited the streamlined "Not one shred of evidence exists that life is serious" to Joseph Campbell; a variant was circulating under Ogden Nash's name by January 2010 per Wayback Machine captures; QI concludes Gill is the originator and the Campbell and Nash connections are not well supported.
Internet Archive holds a scan of Brendan Gill's Here at the New Yorker, catalogued as Random House, New York, 1975, 406 pages, ISBN 0394489896, available through the lending programme.

Brendan Gill lived 4 October 1914 to 27 December 1997, worked at The New Yorker for more than sixty years from 1936, wrote over 1,200 pieces including Profiles, Talk of the Town and Broadway/Off-Broadway reviews, served as the magazine's principal architecture critic writing the Skyline column from 1987 to 1996, published Here at The New Yorker in 1975, and joined Jacqueline Kennedy's coalition to save Grand Central Terminal while chairing the Municipal Art Society and the New York Landmarks Conservancy.

Wikiquote gives Joseph Campbell's dates as 26 March 1904 to 30 October 1987 and describes him as an American professor, writer and orator best known for comparative mythology and comparative religion; the page contains no quote about a "shred of evidence" or "life is serious", and its Disputed section holds only the myth-versus-history line.

Wikiquote gives Ogden Nash's dates as 19 August 1902 to 19 May 1971, and neither "shred of evidence" nor "life is serious" appears on the page; its Misattributed section lists only the "Adam / Had 'em" and pelican verses.

Goodreads hosts "Not one shred of evidence supports the notion that life is serious" attributed to Friedrich Nietzsche with no source book named, alongside the site's notice that quotes are added by the community and are not verified by Goodreads.
Open Library work OL1872271W is Here at the New Yorker by Brendan Gill, first published 1975, original publisher Random House.
Goodreads carries the variant "Not a shred of evidence exists in favor of the idea that life is serious" attributed to Brendan Gill with no source book named.
